answer:
C is not retrying more per request than B: far more of C's first attempts miss their deadline, and every miss re-queues the request. That one fact drives both metrics, because the extra attempts raise retry amplification and add load that produces still more timeouts.

Measured on the same 20 requests/s Poisson workload for 1,800 s after a 300 s warmup with 30 replications: B has retry amplification 1.004, timeout rate 0.0041 and success 0.9996; C has 1.079, 0.111 and 0.9679. Both offer 20 requests/s to 24 requests/s of capacity (12/0.5 s and 18/0.75 s), so nominal capacity and offered-load utilization (0.833) are identical; the difference is resilience headroom, not capacity.

1. Amplification counts realized attempts, not the allowed budget. Retry amplification is total attempts divided by offered requests, so 1.004 means about 0.4% of B's requests made a second attempt even though B may make three, and 1.079 means about 7.9% of C's requests made a second attempt even though C may make only two. B's third attempt is unused headroom; C's second attempt is a routine fallback. Raising the attempt ceiling does not raise amplification unless attempts fail.

2. The deadline-to-service-time ratio sets the first-attempt timeout rate. B's per-attempt timeout is 2.0 s against a 0.5 s lognormal mean (CV 0.6), a 4x ratio; C's is 1.5 s against 0.75 s, a 2x ratio. The deadline starts at arrival and afresh at each retry, and it fires whenever queueing delay plus service exceeds it. Halving the ratio pushes much more of the queueing tail past the deadline. C's p95 of 1.769 s already exceeds its own 1.5 s deadline, which a single attempt cannot do, so C's tail is made of requests that waited through a first attempt plus a backoff; B's p95 of 1.206 s stays well inside its 2.0 s deadline.

3. Retries feed back into load, and timeouts are counted per attempt. C's 7.9% extra attempts raise effective offered load from 20 to about 21.6 requests/s against 24, i.e. utilization from 0.833 to about 0.90, where waiting time rises steeply; B's 0.4% raises it only to about 0.84. C's 11.1% timeout rate is consistent with per-attempt counting: about 7.9% first-attempt timeouts plus about 3.2% second-attempt timeouts that ended the request (success 0.9679 means about 3.2% ended unsuccessfully after at most two attempts), which sums to 11.1%. Each retried-and-failed request therefore contributes two timeout events, so one request population inflates both metrics.

4. Backoff and jitter decide whether retries arrive as a trickle or a synchronized wave. B's exponential backoff (base 0.2 s) uses full jitter; jitter reduces synchronized retry waves, and without it clients that failed together retry together. The comparison records full jitter for B and records no jitter for C, whose declared policy is linear backoff, so C's retries are correlated and arrive as a burst, the documented retry-storm failure mode where a load spike hits the service when it can least absorb it. Those bursts lengthen waits and make the retried attempts themselves likely to miss their deadline.

Net: C's higher amplification and higher timeout rate are two views of one feedback loop. A tight per-attempt deadline turns queueing variance into timeouts; the timeouts become correlated retries that add about 8% load and push utilization toward 0.9; the added load produces more timeouts. B escapes the loop because its few retries are jittered and given twice the deadline headroom, so its three-attempt budget is almost never consumed.

Limits: these are synthetic discrete-event results, not production measurements. The pages read do not state C's service-time coefficient of variation or its linear-backoff base, and the split of C's 11.1% timeout rate into first-attempt and retry components is inferred from the stated definitions rather than reported separately.
